```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(ridge)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

# Introduction

The `ridge` package provides tools for fitting and working with
ridge regression models. It includes model fitting, cross-validation
for selecting the regularization parameter, graphical visualization
of cross-validation errors, and prediction methods.

This vignette presents a complete and reproducible workflow using
the main functions and S3 methods implemented in the package.

# The Ridge Regression Model

Ridge regression is a regularized linear regression method designed
to reduce the magnitude of regression coefficients.

The estimator minimizes the following penalized least-squares
criterion:

\[
\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}
=
\arg\min_{\beta}
\left[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(y_i-\beta_0-x_i^\top\beta)^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2
\right].
\]

Here, \(\lambda\) controls the strength of regularization.
A larger value of \(\lambda\) produces stronger shrinkage
of the explanatory-variable coefficients.

The intercept is not penalized in the implementation
used by this package.

# Generating a Reproducible Dataset

We generate a simulated dataset with two explanatory variables
and a known underlying linear relationship.

```{r data}
set.seed(123)

x <- matrix(rnorm(200), ncol = 2)
colnames(x) <- c("x1", "x2")

y <- 2 + 3 * x[, 1] - x[, 2] + rnorm(100)
```

The data-generating process is:

\[
Y_i = 2 + 3X_{i1} - X_{i2} + \varepsilon_i,
\]

where the error term follows a standard normal distribution.

The theoretical coefficients are therefore 2 for the intercept,
3 for the first explanatory variable, and -1 for the second.

# Fitting a Ridge Model

The `ridge_fit()` function fits a ridge regression model
for a specified regularization parameter.

```{r fitting}
library(ridge)

model <- ridge_fit(
  x = x,
  y = y,
  lambda = 1
)

model
coef(model)
```

The resulting object belongs to the S3 class `ridge_model`.

The estimated coefficients can be compared with the theoretical
values used to generate the data.

```{r model-components}
head(fitted(model))
head(residuals(model))
```

# Cross-Validation

The `ridge_cv()` function performs k-fold cross-validation
over a user-defined grid of regularization parameters.

We consider 50 values of lambda distributed on a logarithmic scale.

```{r cross-validation}
lambda_grid <- 10^seq(-3, 2, length.out = 50)

cv_result <- ridge_cv(
  x = x,
  y = y,
  lambda_grid = lambda_grid,
  k = 5,
  seed = 123
)

cv_result$best_lambda
cv_result$best_mse
```

The selected parameter minimizes the estimated
mean cross-validation error over the specified grid.

# Visualizing Cross-Validation Errors

The S3 plotting method displays the mean cross-validation
error as a function of lambda, together with its standard
error and the selected regularization parameters.

```{r cross-validation-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
selected_parameters <- plot(cv_result)

selected_parameters
```

Two selection criteria are considered:

- The minimum-error criterion selects the lambda associated
  with the smallest estimated cross-validation error.
- The one-standard-error rule selects the largest lambda
  whose estimated error remains within one standard error
  of the minimum.

The latter favors stronger regularization while accepting
a cross-validation error close to the minimum.

# Comparing the Selected Models

We fit two models using the parameters selected by the
two criteria.

```{r model-comparison}
model_min <- ridge_fit(
  x = x,
  y = y,
  lambda = selected_parameters["lambda_min"]
)

model_1se <- ridge_fit(
  x = x,
  y = y,
  lambda = selected_parameters["lambda_1se"]
)

comparison <- cbind(
  Theoretical = c(2, 3, -1),
  Lambda_min = coef(model_min),
  Lambda_1se = coef(model_1se)
)

comparison
```

The Euclidean norms of the explanatory-variable coefficients
can be used to illustrate the shrinkage induced by regularization.

```{r coefficient-norms}
beta_min <- coef(model_min)[-1]
beta_1se <- coef(model_1se)[-1]

sqrt(sum(beta_min^2))
sqrt(sum(beta_1se^2))
```

# Prediction

The `predict()` method allows predictions to be obtained
for new observations.

```{r prediction}
newdata <- x[1:5, , drop = FALSE]

predict(model, newdata = newdata)
```

We can also compare the training mean squared errors
of the two selected models.

```{r training-error}
pred_min <- predict(model_min, newdata = x)
pred_1se <- predict(model_1se, newdata = x)

mse_min <- mean((y - pred_min)^2)
mse_1se <- mean((y - pred_1se)^2)

data.frame(
  Model = c("Minimum CV", "One-standard-error rule"),
  Lambda = c(
    selected_parameters["lambda_min"],
    selected_parameters["lambda_1se"]
  ),
  Training_MSE = c(mse_min, mse_1se)
)
```

These training errors describe the fit on the observations
used for model estimation. They should not be interpreted
as independent estimates of predictive performance.

# Conclusion

The `ridge` package provides a workflow for fitting ridge
regression models, selecting regularization parameters
through cross-validation, visualizing validation errors,
and generating predictions.

The minimum-error and one-standard-error criteria provide
different regularization choices. Their comparison illustrates
the relationship between coefficient shrinkage and model fit.

The examples in this vignette are reproducible and use
a simulated dataset with known theoretical coefficients.
